claim: Mammalian axons are specialized for transmitting action potentials to targets within the central and peripheral nervous system.
source: Mammalian axons are specialized for transmitting action potentials to targets within the central and peripheral nervous system.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that represents established scientific knowledge about axon function.

claim: Axons play essential roles in neural information processing beyond signal conduction.
source: A growing body of evidence suggests that, besides signal conduction, axons play essential roles in neural information processing, and their malfunctions are common hallmarks of neurodegenerative diseases.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to existing literature as indicated by the phrase 'growing body of evidence'.

claim: Axonal malfunctions are common hallmarks of neurodegenerative diseases.
source: A growing body of evidence suggests that, besides signal conduction, axons play essential roles in neural information processing, and their malfunctions are common hallmarks of neurodegenerative diseases.
evidence: This statement references established knowledge about neurodegenerative diseases.

claim: High-density microelectrode arrays (HD-MEAs) allow for accessing axonal action potentials at high spatiotemporal resolution.
source: High-density microelectrode arrays (HD-MEAs) allow for accessing axonal action potentials at high spatiotemporal resolution, but provide no insights on axonal morphology.
evidence: This is a statement about the capabilities of HD-MEA technology, representing established knowledge about the method.

claim: HD-MEAs provide no insights on axonal morphology.
source: High-density microelectrode arrays (HD-MEAs) allow for accessing axonal action potentials at high spatiotemporal resolution, but provide no insights on axonal morphology.
evidence: This represents a limitation of existing HD-MEA technology as understood prior to this study.

claim: The method enabled reconstruction of up to 5-cm-long axonal arbors.
source: The method enabled us to reconstruct up to 5-cm-long axonal arbors and directly monitor axonal conduction across thousands of recording sites.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data.

claim: The method enabled direct monitoring of axonal conduction across thousands of recording sites.
source: The method enabled us to reconstruct up to 5-cm-long axonal arbors and directly monitor axonal conduction across thousands of recording sites.
evidence: This is a primary finding describing the capabilities of the developed method.

claim: A total of 1.86 m of cortical and spinal axons were reconstructed.
source: We reconstructed 1.86 m of cortical and spinal axons in total and found specific features in their structure and function.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's experiments.

claim: Cortical and spinal axons have specific features in their structure and function.
source: We reconstructed 1.86 m of cortical and spinal axons in total and found specific features in their structure and function.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the comparative analysis in the study.

claim: Cortical axons serve as communication cables between various types of neurons that are synaptically connected.
source: Cortical axons serve as communication cables between various types of neurons that are synaptically connected and, accordingly, arranged in multiple layers to receive, process, and convey neural information between different regions in the brain.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about cortical axon function.

claim: Motor neurons located in the ventral horn of the spinal cord project their axons outside the central nervous system.
source: Motor neurons located in the ventral horn of the spinal cord project their axons outside the central nervous system (CNS) and are responsible for the contraction of effector muscles in the periphery.
evidence: This is established anatomical and physiological knowledge about motor neurons.

claim: Spinal axons are specialized to innervate and precisely control different types of muscle fibers.
source: Spinal axons are specialized to innervate and precisely control different types of muscle fibers, thus ensuring refined coordination of complex body movements (Stifani, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Stifani, 2014.

claim: Axons are classically seen as conductive cables that faithfully transmit APs in an all-or-none, 'binary' fashion.
source: Mainly due to difficulties to experimentally access axonal conduction, axonal information processing has been neglected, and axons are classically seen as conductive cables that do nothing more than faithfully transmit APs in an all-or-none, 'binary' fashion (Hodgkin and Huxley, 1952).
evidence: This represents the classical view of axon function, supported by citation to Hodgkin and Huxley, 1952.

claim: Later studies have challenged the classical view that axons only transmit binary signals.
source: Later studies have challenged this view and suggested that axons have much more complex roles than traditionally thought (Alcami and El Hady, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Alcami and El Hady, 2019.

claim: Hippocampal and cortical axons can transmit analog currents in a passive fashion.
source: Contrary to classical concepts, reports show that, besides conducting binary APs, hippocampal and cortical axons can also transmit analog currents in a passive fashion (Shu et al., 2006; Alle and Geiger, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Shu et al., 2006 and Alle and Geiger, 2008.

claim: Analog currents integrate with ongoing axonal APs, changing their waveforms and affecting synaptic transmission in a graded manner.
source: It has been shown that analog currents integrate with ongoing axonal APs, changing their waveforms and, consequently, affecting synaptic transmission in a graded, 'analog' manner (Shu et al., 2006; Alle and Geiger, 2006; Zbili and Debanne, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Shu et al., 2006; Alle and Geiger, 2006; and Zbili and Debanne, 2019.

claim: Axons modulate the waveforms of APs contingent on neuronal activity and adjust the synaptic release.
source: Additionally, it was found that axons modulate the waveforms of APs contingent on neuronal activity and, accordingly, adjust the synaptic release (Geiger and Jonas, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Geiger and Jonas, 2000.

claim: During high-frequency regimes of neuronal activity, axons can reduce their conduction velocities by more than 20%.
source: Moreover, during high-frequency regimes of neuronal activity, axons are able to reduce their conduction velocities by more than 20% and, thereby, tune the timing of AP arrival at synapses (Radivojevic et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Radivojevic et al., 2017.

claim: Cortical axons have diameters of 0.08–0.4 μm.
source: Due to their small diameter of 0.08–0.4 μm (Debanne, 2004) and absence of surrounding myelin sheaths, cortical axons provide relatively low conduction velocities of 0.1–2 m/s (Radivojevic et al., 2017; Bakkum et al., 2013), which are, nevertheless, sufficient to ensure rapid communication between closely spaced neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Debanne, 2004.

claim: Cortical axons provide conduction velocities of 0.1–2 m/s.
source: Due to their small diameter of 0.08–0.4 μm (Debanne, 2004) and absence of surrounding myelin sheaths, cortical axons provide relatively low conduction velocities of 0.1–2 m/s (Radivojevic et al., 2017; Bakkum et al., 2013), which are, nevertheless, sufficient to ensure rapid communication between closely spaced neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Radivojevic et al., 2017 and Bakkum et al., 2013.

claim: Motor neuron axons can be up to 1 m long.
source: As opposed to cortical neurons, motor neurons transmit signals to distant targets outside the CNS and, for that purpose, develop considerably longer (up to 1 m), thicker (0.5–10 μm), and myelinated axons that provide considerably higher conduction velocities of up to 100 m/s (Debanne et al., 2011; Saliani et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Debanne et al., 2011 and Saliani et al., 2017.

claim: Motor neuron axons have diameters of 0.5–10 μm.
source: As opposed to cortical neurons, motor neurons transmit signals to distant targets outside the CNS and, for that purpose, develop considerably longer (up to 1 m), thicker (0.5–10 μm), and myelinated axons that provide considerably higher conduction velocities of up to 100 m/s (Debanne et al., 2011; Saliani et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Debanne et al., 2011 and Saliani et al., 2017.

claim: Myelinated motor neuron axons provide conduction velocities of up to 100 m/s.
source: As opposed to cortical neurons, motor neurons transmit signals to distant targets outside the CNS and, for that purpose, develop considerably longer (up to 1 m), thicker (0.5–10 μm), and myelinated axons that provide considerably higher conduction velocities of up to 100 m/s (Debanne et al., 2011; Saliani et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Debanne et al., 2011 and Saliani et al., 2017.

claim: Conduction failures are likely to occur at axonal branching points and local swellings due to abruptly increased axon diameter.
source: For instance, experimental and theoretical studies suggest that conduction failures are likely to occur at axonal branching points and local swellings due to abruptly increased axon diameter (Debanne, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Debanne, 2004.

claim: Thin distal axons (diameter <1 μm) are prone to 'channel noise'.
source: According to theoretical studies, thin distal axons (diameter <1 μm) are prone to 'channel noise', which can introduce variability in axonal AP waveforms (Neishabouri and Faisal, 2014), increase the jitter of AP propagation (Radivojevic et al., 2017; Faisal and Laughlin, 2007), and compromise the reliability of the conduction itself (Faisal and Laughlin, 2007; Skaugen and Walløe, 1979; Schneidman et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Neishabouri and Faisal, 2014; Radivojevic et al., 2017; Faisal and Laughlin, 2007; Skaugen and Walløe, 1979; and Schneidman et al., 1998.

claim: High-frequency neuronal activity increases the jitter of AP propagation in cortical axons.
source: Besides geometrical factors, neuronal activity can also affect AP conduction, which is consistent with our previous finding that high-frequency neuronal activity increases the jitter of AP propagation in cortical axons (Radivojevic et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Radivojevic et al., 2017.

claim: In Alzheimer's disease, abnormal protein aggregates cause local swellings in axons which reduce conduction velocity and block AP propagation.
source: For instance, in Alzheimer's disease (AD), abnormal protein aggregates cause local swellings in axons which have been shown to reduce conduction velocity and even block AP propagation (Blazquez-Llorca et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Blazquez-Llorca et al., 2017.

claim: Axonal degeneration may be the earliest feature of Parkinson's disease.
source: Human post-mortem studies suggest that axonal degeneration may be the earliest feature of Parkinson's disease and, therefore, an appropriate target for early therapeutic interventions (Burke and O'Malley, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Burke and O'Malley, 2013.

claim: In amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, axonal dysfunction begins long before symptom onset and motor neuron death.
source: Motor neuron degeneration is the hallmark of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), where axonal dysfunction begins long before symptom onset and motor neuron death (Suzuki et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Suzuki et al., 2020.

claim: The whole-cell patch-clamp technique is typically limited to recording APs from a single axonal site.
source: However, patch-clamp is typically limited to recording APs from a single axonal site (Shu et al., 2006; Alle and Geiger, 2006; Forsythe, 1994) and does not allow for tracking AP propagation across axons.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Shu et al., 2006; Alle and Geiger, 2006; and Forsythe, 1994.

claim: Fluorescent indicators exhibit photobleaching and phototoxicity and may perturb the physiology of the cell.
source: However, fluorescent indicators exhibit photobleaching and phototoxicity and may perturb the physiology of the cell to the point of affecting AP conduction (Peterka et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Peterka et al., 2011.

claim: HD-MEAs enable detection of APs across entire arbors of cortical axons, including tiny axon terminals.
source: Thanks to a low-noise CMOS design, HD-MEAs enable detection of APs across entire arbors of cortical axons, including tiny axon terminals (Radivojevic et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Radivojevic et al., 2017.

claim: Live-cell imaging techniques entail introduction of fluorescent reporters into the cell, which induces chemotoxicity, phototoxicity, and cell death.
source: These techniques, however, entail introduction of fluorescent reporters into the cell, which induces chemotoxicity, phototoxicity, and cell death (Icha et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Icha et al., 2017.

claim: The method allows for label-free electrical visualization of axonal conduction trajectories.
source: The method allows for label-free electrical visualization of axonal conduction trajectories and, at the same time, provides noninvasive access to axonal APs waveforms recorded across hundreds of microelectrodes.
evidence: This is a primary finding describing the capabilities of the developed method.

claim: The reconstructed morphology reveals the location of the axon initial segment (AIS), axonal trunk, and higher-order branches.
source: The reconstructed morphology is here referred to as 'functional morphology', and it reveals the location of the axon initial segment (AIS), axonal trunk, and higher-order branches (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding describing what the functional morphology reveals, supported by Figure 1B.

claim: The utilized HD-MEA system features 26,400 microelectrodes packed within an area of 3.85×2.1 mm².
source: The utilized HD-MEA system features 26,400 microelectrodes packed within an area of 3.85×2.1 mm2.
evidence: This is a technical specification of the HD-MEA system used in the study, shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Interelectrode distances of 17.5 μm provide density of 3264 microelectrodes per mm².
source: Interelectrode distances of 17.5 μm provide density of 3264 microelectrodes per mm2.
evidence: This is a technical specification of the HD-MEA system, shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Neuronal extracellular action potentials were recorded at 20 kHz sampling rate.
source: Neuronal extracellular action potentials (APs) were recorded through HD-MEA recording channels at 20 kHz sampling rate.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the recording parameters, shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Cortical cultures were grown in monolayers with estimated thicknesses of ~5–40 μm.
source: The cultures were grown in monolayers with estimated thicknesses of ~5–40 and ~5–50 μm for cortical and motor neuron cultures, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a measurement from the experimental cultures, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Motor neuron cultures were grown in monolayers with estimated thicknesses of ~5–50 μm.
source: The cultures were grown in monolayers with estimated thicknesses of ~5–40 and ~5–50 μm for cortical and motor neuron cultures, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a measurement from the experimental cultures, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Both cortical and motor neuron cultures yielded cell densities of ~500–2000 neurons per mm².
source: Both cortical and motor neuron cultures yielded cell densities of ~500–2000 neurons per mm2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a measurement from the experimental cultures, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: The relative proximity of axons to the sensing area varied within ranges of ~1–13 μm for cortical neurons.
source: The relative proximity of axons to the sensing area varied across axonal arbors within ranges of ~1–13 and ~1–18 μm for cortical and motor neurons, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is a measurement from the experimental cultures, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: The relative proximity of axons to the sensing area varied within ranges of ~1–18 μm for motor neurons.
source: The relative proximity of axons to the sensing area varied across axonal arbors within ranges of ~1–13 and ~1–18 μm for cortical and motor neurons, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is a measurement from the experimental cultures, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: The AIS is the dominant contributor to the neuron's extracellular electrical landscape.
source: It has been previously shown that the AIS is the dominant contributor to the neuron's extracellular electrical landscape (Bakkum et al., 2019), which can be attributed to the high densities of voltage-gated ion channels expressed in the AIS (Kole et al., 2008; Hu et al., 2009; Lorincz and Nusser, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bakkum et al., 2019; Kole et al., 2008; Hu et al., 2009; and Lorincz and Nusser, 2010.

claim: The algorithm could detect 45%, 74%, and 98% of the actual peaks after the first, second, and third steps, respectively.
source: We were able to detect 45%, 74%, and 98% of the actual peaks after the first, second, and third steps, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the validation analysis, shown in Figure 5B.

claim: No false peak detections were observed for thresholds set to 9, 2, and 1 STD of the noise in first, second, and third steps, respectively.
source: We observed no false peak detections for thresholds set to 9, 2, and 1 STD of the noise in first, second, and third steps, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the validation analysis, shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The algorithm could interconnect 70%, 85%, and 91% of the mapped AP peaks after the first, second, and third steps, respectively.
source: We could interconnect 70%, 85%, and 91% of the mapped AP peaks after the first, second, and third steps, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the validation analysis, shown in Figure 6B.

claim: No false links were established when using the interconnection areas with diameters of 100, 200, and 400 μm in first, second, and third steps, respectively.
source: We observed no false links when using the interconnection areas with diameters of 100, 200, and 400 μm in first, second, and third steps, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the validation analysis, shown in Figure 6B.

claim: A total length of 1.04 m of cortical axons was reconstructed from 50 neurons.
source: We reconstructed functional morphologies for 50 cortical and 50 motor neurons and analyzed morphological features of their axonal arbors, a total length of 1.04 m and 0.81 m of cortical and spinal axons, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's experiments.

claim: A total length of 0.81 m of spinal axons was reconstructed from 50 neurons.
source: We reconstructed functional morphologies for 50 cortical and 50 motor neurons and analyzed morphological features of their axonal arbors, a total length of 1.04 m and 0.81 m of cortical and spinal axons, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's experiments.

claim: The average axonal lengths were 16.73±1.20 mm for cortical neurons and 14.63±0.88 mm for motor neurons (p=0.25).
source: The average axonal lengths were 16.73±1.20 and 14.63±0.88 mm for cortical and motor neurons, respectively (p=0.25).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the comparative analysis, shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Ratios between axonal lengths and their corresponding active areas were significantly higher for cortical than spinal axons.
source: However, ratios between axonal lengths and their corresponding active areas were significantly higher for cortical than spinal axons (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the comparative analysis, shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The average length-to-area quotients were 11.72±0.32 mm⁻¹ for cortical neurons and 9.49±0.24 mm⁻¹ for motor neurons (p<10⁻⁶).
source: The average length-to-area quotients were 11.72±0.32 and 9.49±0.24 mm–1 for cortical and motor neurons, respectively (p<10–6).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the comparative analysis, shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Cortical axons develop branching points in more proximal parts of their arbors compared to spinal axons.
source: We found cortical axons to develop branching points in more proximal parts of their arbors and to form shorter inter-branching segments as compared to spinal axons (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the comparative analysis, shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Average axial distances of axonal branching points were 0.27±0.01 mm for cortical neurons and 0.43±0.01 mm for motor neurons (p<10⁻⁶).
source: Average axial distances of axonal branching points were 0.27±0.01 and 0.43±0.01 mm for cortical and motor neurons, respectively (p<10–6).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the comparative analysis, shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Average lengths of axonal inter-branching segments were 0.34±0.01 mm for cortical neurons and 0.48±0.01 mm for motor neurons (p<10⁻⁶).
source: Average lengths of axonal inter-branching segments were 0.34±0.01 and 0.48±0.01 mm for cortical and motor neurons, respectively (p<10–6).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the comparative analysis, shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Cortical axons have significantly more axon terminals than spinal axons.
source: We found significantly more axon terminals in cortical than in spinal axons; however, spinal axons projected their terminals at significantly greater distances as compared to cortical axons (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the comparative analysis, shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Average numbers of axon terminals were 29.92±1.64 for cortical neurons and 17.82±1.03 for motor neurons (p<10⁻⁶).
source: Average numbers of axon terminals were 29.92±1.64 and 17.82±1.03 for cortical and motor neurons, respectively (p<10–6).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the comparative analysis, shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Average axial distances of axon terminals were 1.17±0.02 mm for cortical neurons and 2.41±0.04 mm for motor neurons (p<10⁻⁶).
source: Average axial distances of axon terminals were 1.17±0.02 and 2.41±0.04 mm for cortical and motor neurons, respectively (p<10–6).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the comparative analysis, shown in Figure 7D.

claim: APs recorded from proximal axons had significantly higher amplitude in cortical (44.58±4.81 µV) than in motor neurons (19.07±2.53 µV; p<10⁻⁶).
source: APs recorded from proximal axons had significantly higher amplitude in cortical (44.58±4.81 µV) than in motor neurons (19.07±2.53 µV; p<10–6).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the comparative analysis, shown in Figure 8B.

claim: APs recorded from distal axons had significantly smaller amplitude in cortical (1.50±0.10 µV) than in motor neurons (3.30±0.38 µV; p<10⁻⁶).
source: On the contrary, APs recorded from distal axons had significantly smaller amplitude in cortical (1.50±0.10 µV) than in motor neurons (3.30±0.38 µV; p<10–6; Figure 8B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the comparative analysis, shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Average amplitudes of APs recorded from primary axonal trunks were 33.29±4.78 µV for cortical neurons and 15.06±2.78 µV for motor neurons (p=0.002).
source: Average amplitudes of APs recorded from primary axonal trunks were 33.29±4.78 and 15.06±2.78 µV for cortical and motor neurons, respectively (p=0.002).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the comparative analysis, shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Average amplitudes of APs recorded from axonal trees were 1.25±0.13 µV for cortical neurons and 2.17±0.30 µV for motor neurons (p=0.024).
source: Average amplitudes of APs recorded from axonal trees were 1.25±0.13 and 2.17±0.30 µV for cortical and motor neurons, respectively (p=0.024).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the comparative analysis, shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Cortical neurons had significantly shorter active timespans than motor neurons.
source: Cortical neurons had significantly shorter active timespans and higher synchronization of the arrival times as compared to motor neurons (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the comparative analysis, shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Active timespans were 4.60±0.33 ms for cortical neurons and 7.40±0.32 ms for motor neurons (p<10⁻⁶).
source: Active timespans were 4.60±0.33 and 7.40±0.32 ms for cortical and motor neurons, respectively (p<10–6).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the comparative analysis, shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Intervals of signal arrivals at axon terminals were 3.44±0.31 ms for cortical neurons and 5.40±0.34 ms for motor neurons (p=0.0024).
source: Intervals of signal arrivals at axon terminals were 3.44±0.31 and 5.40±0.34 ms for cortical and motor neurons, respectively (p=0.0024).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the comparative analysis, shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Variance of signal arrival times were 0.95±0.23 ms² for cortical neurons and 2.50±0.35 ms² for motor neurons (p<10⁻⁴).
source: Variance of signal arrival times were 0.95±0.23 and 2.50±0.35 ms2 for cortical and motor neurons, respectively (p<10–4).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the comparative analysis, shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Cortical axons exhibit significantly slower conduction velocities compared to spinal axons.
source: We found cortical axons to exhibit significantly slower and more uniform conduction velocities compared to spinal axons (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the comparative analysis, shown in Figure 9C.

claim: Average conduction velocities were 0.46±0.01 m/s for cortical neurons and 0.56±0.02 m/s for motor neurons (p<10⁻⁴).
source: Average conduction velocities were 0.46±0.01 and 0.56±0.02 m/s for cortical and motor neurons, respectively (p<10–4).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the comparative analysis, shown in Figure 9C.

claim: Variances of conduction velocities were 0.03±0.002 m/s for cortical neurons and 0.04±0.003 m/s for motor neurons (p<10⁻⁴).
source: Variances of conduction velocities were 0.03±0.002 and 0.04±0.003 m/s for cortical and motor neurons, respectively (p<10–4).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the comparative analysis, shown in Figure 9C.

claim: The CMOS-based HD-MEA system comprises 26,400 platinum microelectrodes packed within an area of 3.85×2.10 mm².
source: The array comprises 26,400 platinum microelectrodes (9.3×5.45 μm2) packed within an area of 3.85×2.10 mm2, providing a density of 3150 electrodes per mm2 (17.5 μm center-to-center pitch).
evidence: This is a technical specification of the HD-MEA system used in the study.

claim: Up to 1024 readout and/or stimulation channels could be routed to the desired electrodes.
source: Owing to a flexible switch matrix technology, up to 1024 readout and/or stimulation channels could be routed to the desired electrodes and reconfigured within a few milliseconds.
evidence: This is a technical specification of the HD-MEA system used in the study.

claim: Cortices from embryonic day 18 Sprague Dawley rat were used for cortical neuron cultures.
source: Cortices from embryonic day 18 Sprague Dawley rat were dissociated enzymatically in trypsin supplemented with 0.25% EDTA (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and physically by trituration.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the source of cortical neurons.

claim: Spinal cords isolated from embryonic day 14 Sprague Dawley rat were used for motor neuron cultures.
source: Spinal cords isolated from embryonic day 14 Sprague Dawley rat were dissociated enzymatically in trypsin supplemented with 0.25% EDTA (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and physically by trituration.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the source of motor neurons.

claim: All experimental protocols were approved by the Uppsala Animal Ethical Committee under animal license C97/15.
source: All experimental protocols were approved by the Uppsala Animal Ethical Committee under animal license C97/15 and follow the guidelines of the Swedish Legislation on Animal Experimentation (Animal Welfare Act SFS 2009:303) and the European Communities Council Directive (2010/63/EU).
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval for the study.
